report:
# Evidence Assessment: Chlorhexidine-Alcohol vs. Iodine-Alcohol for Cesarean Skin Prep

Your claim is well-supported by the evidence, though with some nuance across studies.

**Strongest evidence:** The largest and most rigorous trial is a randomized trial published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* (Tuuli et al.), which found that chlorhexidine-alcohol resulted in a "significantly lower risk of surgical-site infection after cesarean delivery than did the use of iodine-alcohol" (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048). A separate trial reported in the *International Journal of Reproduction, Contraception, Obstetrics and Gynecology* found SSI rates of 6.95% (chlorhexidine) vs. 14.28% (iodine), a statistically significant difference (P=0.005) (https://www.ijrcog.org/index.php/ijrcog/article/view/6461).

**Supporting meta-analysis:** A systematic review and meta-analysis in *PubMed* pooling multiple RCTs also concluded chlorhexidine-alcohol reduces SSI compared to povidone-iodine (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/).

**Some caveats:** Not all individual trials reached statistical significance. A pilot RCT found chlorhexidine trended toward fewer infections but "did not reach statistical significance" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8369632/). Additionally, a more recent 2024 network meta-analysis (published in the *Journal of Hospital Infection*) suggested "either can be used" given the paucity of high-quality head-to-head data, indicating some remaining uncertainty despite the overall trend favoring chlorhexidine.

**Conclusion:** The preponderance of evidence, especially the large NEJM trial and cumulative meta-analyses, supports chlorhexidine-alcohol as superior to iodine-alcohol for reducing SSI after cesarean delivery. This has led to its adoption as a preferred practice in many settings, though some individual studies show non-significant trends and at least one meta-analysis urges caution before declaring definitive superiority.
